To change the key.

Tune to EADGBE

Place capo on 3rd fret.

Play a D chord - just like you would without a capo.

You're now playing a D in the key of G. No, I'm not kidding. "Everyone, let's do this next one in G!" Rather than sit there and fuck around, toss the capo on the 3rd fret and play it the same damned way you were gonna play it in the first place. Tada! You fit in and you changed the key for another instrument that's limited in the key it plays in (like a harmonica) or changed it for the vocalist.

There are other uses, as well. You can turn your guitar from being 24" to one that's 23.25". That's the distance between the nut and the bridge. It makes your scales shorter.

Then, there's fancy stuff you can do. I have capos that will fret multiple frets and leave some open - they're adjustable.

I highly, highly recommend getting a capo. In fact, I recommend getting a half dozen of 'em! For most folks, two or three is enough. If you're spending more than $25 on them, you're spending too much. Just cheap capos, of two types. You have the spring type and the locking nut type. I'd get one of each and a spare of your preference - most like the spring type, as it's faster and you can just clip it to your headstock when you're done using it.

You won't be surprised, not even a little bit, to learn I own a surprising number of them. That should surprise you exactly none.

Since then, a little leeway has opened up on the subject. Even New York Times columnist Thomas Friedman, a staunch advocate for Israel, has conceded the lobby's existence.

In 2011, he explained a well-established, if astounding, ritual of US politics: that the Congress greets every visiting Israeli prime minister more rapturously than the American president himself.

Friedman observed: "I sure hope that Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, understands that the standing ovation he got in Congress this year was not for his politics. That ovation was bought and paid for by the Israel lobby."
